modular.name: Modular structure
modular.text:
Inspect the supplied codebase and identify its core component: the connected set of responsibilities around which the application's main behavior and state are organized. Generate a single ASCII tree diagram showing that core component's modular structure: its logical modules, what each exposes and keeps internal, and how they depend on one another. Choose the scope and level of detail that best explain the codebase. Ground the diagram in the source code.

Structure the tree as a modular decomposition of the core component:
  - Top-level branches are the core's main modules: logical-semantic groupings of responsibility, not directories or files. Each module appears in exactly one place.
  - Depth always means "belongs to": a child is a submodule, type or function grouped within its parent's responsibility.
  - Abstract away file-level organization, but keep boundaries: under each module, distinguish what it exposes to other modules from what it keeps internal.
  - Place dependency lines under the module that depends, with -> lines to the modules it uses. Other relationships appear only where they explain a boundary; do not organize the tree around them.
Cover breadth before depth:
  - Name every major module of the core, even in one line, before detailing any of them.
  - When a module has substantial internal structure, give it a child line naming its submodules, even if you do not expand them.
  - Do not detail one module down to individual helpers or fields while another major module remains a single line.

call.name: Call
call.text:
Inspect the supplied codebase and identify its core component: the connected set of responsibilities around which the application's main behavior and state are organized. Generate a single ASCII tree diagram showing that core component's call structure: the main operations it performs and which activations invoke which. Choose the scope and level of detail that best explain the codebase. Ground the diagram in the source code.

Structure the tree as a call decomposition of the core component:
  - Top-level branches are the core's main operations: the entry points or recurring loops through which its behavior happens. Each operation appears in exactly one place; when another flow re-enters it, reference it by name.
  - Depth always means "is invoked during": a child is a call made by, or a step performed within, its parent activation. List siblings in execution order.
  - Show synchronous calls and asynchronous hand-offs (queues, events, workers, timers) distinctly. Show decisions as sibling branches under the step that makes them, and loops once with their exit condition.
  - Other relationships appear only as brief -> lines where they change the flow; do not organize the tree around modules or owners.
Cover breadth before depth:
  - Name every main operation of the core, even in one line, before tracing any of them.
  - When a call triggers a substantial flow of its own, give it a child line naming that flow's phases, even if you do not expand them.
  - Do not trace one operation down to individual helper calls while another main operation remains a single line.

ownership.name: Ownership
ownership.text:
Inspect the supplied codebase and identify its core component: the connected set of responsibilities around which the application's main behavior and state are organized. Generate a single ASCII tree diagram showing that core component's ownership structure: who creates, retains, changes and releases its state, storage and resources, and their lifetimes. Choose the scope and level of detail that best explain the codebase. Ground the diagram in the source code.

Structure the tree as an ownership decomposition of the core component:
  - Top-level branches are the core's root owners: the long-lived holders from which its other state and resources hang. Each owned thing appears in exactly one place, under its owner.
  - Depth always means "is owned by": a child is created, retained or released by its parent, and does not outlive it unless handed off.
  - Under each owner, state when its children are created, changed and released. Show borrowed or shared references as -> lines to their owner, not as children.
  - Other relationships appear only where they explain a lifetime; do not organize the tree around calls or modules.
Cover breadth before depth:
  - Name every major owner in the core, even in one line, before detailing any of them.
  - When an owner holds substantial state of its own, give it a child line naming what it holds, even if you do not expand it.
  - Do not detail one owner down to field layouts, allocators or buffers while another major owner remains a single line.

data.name: Data dependency
data.text:
Inspect the supplied codebase and identify its core component: the connected set of responsibilities around which the application's main behavior and state are organized. Generate a single ASCII tree diagram showing that core component's data dependencies: what each of its results actually needs in order to be computed. Choose the scope and level of detail that best explain the codebase. Ground the diagram in the source code.

Structure the tree as a data-dependency decomposition of the core component:
  - Top-level branches are the core's main results: the values, states or outputs it exists to produce. Each derived value is expanded in exactly one place; where it is needed again, reference it by name.
  - Depth always means "is computed from": a child is an input its parent needs, and its own children are what that input needs in turn.
  - Under each value, name the computation that combines its inputs into it. Mark inputs that come from outside the core (user input, files, network, configuration) as leaves.
  - Other relationships appear only where they explain a dependency; do not organize the tree around calls, modules or owners.
Cover breadth before depth:
  - Name every main result of the core, even in one line, before tracing any of them.
  - When an input has substantial derivation of its own, give it a child line naming what it is derived from, even if you do not expand it.
  - Do not trace one result down to individual fields or bytes while another main result remains a single line.
